topic: The DoorDash vs Uber Eats Split
description: A timeline comparison of how DoorDash surged while Uber Eats stumbled—driven by quick delivery scale, restaurant coverage, and shifting unit economics from 2019 through 2025 (with 2026 estimates).
youtube_description:
🍿 *The DoorDash vs Uber Eats Split* — a chart-race timeline of how “fast growth” turned into a market-leader problem.

00:00 — 2019: DoorDash scales aggressively as delivery moves from convenience to habit.
01:10 — 2020: The pandemic accelerates GOV for DoorDash and boosts Uber Eats—but DoorDash’s restaurant density compounds faster.
02:25 — 2021: DoorDash’s momentum peaks as it expands ordering frequency and driver/merchant supply.
03:40 — 2022: Costs rise across the sector; Uber Eats flattens while DoorDash maintains share.
04:55 — 2023: Uber Eats growth slows as incentives tighten; DoorDash continues climbing.
06:15 — 2024: DoorDash pulls further ahead; legacy brands (Grubhub, Postmates) keep shrinking.
07:30 — 2025: The “winner-take-more” effect shows up in the gap—DoorDash keeps adding scale.
08:40 — 2026 (estimate): Projection adds a punchy final sprint for DoorDash, while Uber Eats stabilizes.

Why this matters: every line here represents consumer habit + restaurant coverage + unit economics pressure—not just “who has the app.” Watch how DoorDash turns survival years into a domination window.

If you want more viral chart-race breakdowns, LIKE, SUBSCRIBE, and comment what market we should compare next.

Sources (industry reporting): DoorDash quarterly financial filings; Uber annual reports and 10-Ks (for marketplace gross bookings context); historical transaction and brand consolidation milestones for Grubhub and Postmates.

instagram_caption:
🚀 DoorDash just kept sprinting while Uber Eats started to level off—here’s the split timeline in numbers.

In 2019, DoorDash was already on the rise: about $15B in Marketplace Gross Order Value (GOV) as food delivery shifted from “nice-to-have” to “default.” Uber Eats (via Uber’s Gross Bookings) was bigger at roughly $25B, with the broader Uber brand helping it stay the mainstream choice.

Then 2020 hit—everything changed. DoorDash jumped to about $35B GOV as the pandemic locked in routine orders. Uber Eats also surged, climbing to around $38B. But notice the difference: DoorDash didn’t just grow with demand; it scaled merchant coverage and ordering frequency fast enough that the gap started to form even during the boom.

By 2021, DoorDash reached roughly $55B GOV, while Uber Eats moved to about $48B. That’s the turning point: DoorDash’s growth curve steepened while Uber Eats began showing early signs of flattening under incentive pressure. In 2022, DoorDash kept expanding to about $68B GOV, but Uber Eats only inched to around $52B.

2023–2025 is where the chart race gets brutal. DoorDash accelerates from about $78B (2023) to $101B (2025). Uber Eats rises more slowly—about $54B (2023) to $59B (2025). Meanwhile, the “background runners” got crushed: Grubhub drops from about $10B (2019) to ~$1B by 2025, and Postmates falls from about $6B (2019) to ~$0.4B by 2025 as consolidation reshaped the delivery map.

So the story isn’t only “who grew.” It’s who kept growing *after* the easy demand wave passed.

📌 Question for you: In your city, did DoorDash become the default because it had better selection, faster delivery, or better prices?

DoorDash’s rise versus Uber Eats is best understood as a timeline of compounding advantages rather than a single “win.” Starting in 2019, DoorDash tracked at roughly $15B in Marketplace Gross Order Value (GOV), behind Uber Eats’ about $25B in Gross Bookings. During the pandemic in 2020, both increased sharply—DoorDash to ~$35B and Uber Eats to ~$38B—reflecting broad demand growth.

The divergence appears by 2021–2022. DoorDash accelerates to approximately $55B in 2021 and $68B in 2022, while Uber Eats flattens more noticeably, moving to ~$48B in 2021 and ~$52B in 2022. From 2023 onward, the gap becomes dramatic: DoorDash reaches about $78B (2023) and climbs to ~$101B by 2025, whereas Uber Eats rises from ~$54B (2023) to ~$59B (2025). 

At the same time, legacy brands contract sharply as consolidation reshapes consumer choice. Grubhub declines from about $10B in 2019 to roughly $1B by 2025, and Postmates falls from about $6B in 2019 to about $0.4B by 2025. The overall pattern suggests that DoorDash’s merchant density and repeat ordering created a durable growth engine while Uber Eats faced more friction balancing incentives, costs, and scale.
